wstep: This card follows the University of Georgia (UGA) raspberry vinegar recipe from its suggested flavorings: raspberries steeped in commercially produced vinegar, strained and kept in the refrigerator.

akapity: It covers only the steeped version; homemade fermented (“live”) vinegar is not covered, because flavored vinegars should be made only with commercially produced vinegar.
For one quart jar: 2 cups fresh raspberries and 3 cups vinegar.
Apple cider vinegar blends best with fruits, according to UGA.
For added safety, use only commercially produced vinegar.
Wine and rice vinegars contain some protein that is an excellent medium for bacterial growth if they are not handled and stored properly.
Vinegar with less than 5% acidity should never be used in home food preservation.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not replace it with a stronger vinegar and do not dilute a stronger vinegar with water yourself; Penn State Extension advises staying within 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and diluting vinegar only when a tested recipe says so.
Do not add more flavoring than this card gives: too much plant material can destroy the acid and ruin the preservative quality of the vinegar.
A US pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
Wash glass jars or bottles in warm, soapy water, then sterilize them by immersing them completely in boiling water for 10 minutes; fill them with vinegar while they are still warm.

Close them with non-corrodible metal or plastic screw caps, washed in hot soapy water, rinsed and scalded in boiling water, or with new, pre-sterilized corks dipped in and out of boiling water with tongs 3–4 times.
Work in a very clean area with sanitized utensils and very clean hands.
Wash the raspberries gently but thoroughly and bruise them slightly with the back of a spoon.
Place them in a sterilized quart glass canning jar.
Heat the vinegar to just below the boiling point, to at least 190–195 °F (88–91 °C), and pour it over the raspberries.
Cap the jar tightly and let it stand for 2 to 3 weeks in a cool, dark place.
Strain the vinegar through damp cheesecloth and discard the fruit; if it is still cloudy, strain it again, for example through a coffee filter.
Pour the vinegar into clean, sterilized glass jars or bottles and seal them tightly.
Label each bottle with the base vinegar, the flavoring and the date.
Store the vinegar in the refrigerator for best quality and flavor.
Keep the vinegar in the refrigerator: some harmful bacteria may survive and even multiply slowly in some vinegars.
Fruit vinegars may start to brown and change flavor noticeably after 3 months in cool storage.
For best quality, use it within 4–6 months, as OSU Extension advises for flavored vinegars.
Date the bottle when you open it.
Bottles kept as decorations on sunny window sills or shelves for more than a few weeks should be treated as decorations and not used in food.
If the vinegar shows mold or signs of fermentation such as bubbling, cloudiness or sliminess, throw it away without tasting it.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not use this fruit vinegar for making pickles; OSU allows flavored herb vinegar for pickle making only when it has a 5% acidity level.
